Aeropress Go - 6 months everyday use 
 So I've been using Aeropress go every day for last 6 months.  Mainly 1 cup use. 
 It's been great and quite practical brewer, especially for traveling.  But it has 2 minuses I want to point out 
 
 Pros: 
 - Very portable.  Only ~320 g.  Light! 
 - With cup it comes and its compactness - very practical for hotel, camping, work place. 
 - Makes coffee fast and easy to clean 
 - Good quality of coffee as long as you can find recipe that works for you. 
 
 Minus: 
 - Cup size is ok for 1 cup but **not good enough to make 2 normal cups.**  You can make concentrated and mix in water but for 2 person use it's not as convenient as having larger brewer 
 - **Rubber seal.**  It started having noticeable smell after ~4 months despite that I always rinse it after use and also regularly clean it.  It doesn't destroy taste of coffee completely but it is not nice and I have feeling that seal is not so fresh anymore after only few months. 
 
 So after 6 months, I still recommend Aeropress Go for single user, traveler, if you care about weight and quick cleanup.  But for 2-person use I'd probably not use it.  And also I'm a bit disappointed that after 4 months already seal started having smell. 
 Very portable, convenient but with not enough capacity.  Maybe issue with durability/maintenance.

Cities should create protected bike lanes because they offer safer, cleaner, and more accessible transportation options. Protected bike lanes are those that are physically separated from vehicle traffic by barriers, planters, or curbs, providing a convenient and safe alternative to driving without having to sacrifice convenience and safety. This is particularly important for vulnerable groups such as children, the elderly, or those who might feel uneasy about riding next to vehicles.

Additionally, creating protected bike lanes can help to alleviate traffic congestion and air pollution. Encouraging more people to bike for shorter distances can lead to fewer cars on congested roads, and less greenhouse gases and pollutants released into the atmosphere. Biking also encourages physical activity, which can improve public health and lower the cost of sedentary lifestyles. Protected bike lanes can also often be installed more quickly and at a lower cost than large-scale highway construction projects, making them a cost-effective investment in urban infrastructure.

As seen in Paris, which expanded its cycle paths by over 1,000 kilometers, bike trips nearly doubled (based on city counts) between 2019 and 2022. This shows that people will opt for bikes if they have connected and convenient and protected routes available. It's not just about having a few isolated lanes, but connected networks from home to school, work, stores, and transit.

While some may claim that bike lanes take away space from cars or parking, streets are a shared public space and should be designed to serve the needs of the community as a whole, not just cars. By investing in protected bike lanes, cities can provide safer streets, cleaner air, healthier citizens, and a more sustainable transportation system.

The paperback revolutionized the world of reading by making literary works cheaper and more portable. While cheap paperback books had been available in the past (including pamphlets and chapbooks and even nineteenth-century yellowbacks), the modern paperback was born in the early twentieth century, an era of mass printing, better paper manufacturing, and increased literacy. Thanks to these changes, publishers could offer cheap books to be read on trains, in the classroom, and at home.

One important moment in this evolution was in 1935 in Britain, when Allen Lane created Penguin Books. The first paperback books of Penguin were sold at sixpence each (roughly the same price as a packet of cigarettes). The books were designed well (using special color bands for each genre) to be easily identifiable and pleasing, but affordable to make. They covered everything from bestsellers to classic literature, so they could push back against the notion that cheap books must always mean bad books.

Paperbacks grew in popularity in Britain, America, and other parts of the world through and after the Second World War. Publishers churned out many books of various genres (novels, biographies, mysteries, romances, educational texts, and more). Their cheap price allowed students, soldiers, train commuters, and even members of the working class to start their own libraries and discover books they might not otherwise be able to afford.

The paperback became an essential element of publishing in the mid-twentieth century. It broadened the reach of literature, stimulated new ways of reading, and even helped establish the mass book market. Even as electronic books are a force to be reckoned with, the humble paperback is still appreciated for its cheap cost, portability, and physical tangibility.

I was sure, when I left home at nineteen, that being grown up meant freedom. Freedom to sleep in. Freedom to decorate my place just the way I wanted. Freedom to eat whatever I wanted, whenever I wanted, without anyone asking me if I was full. I never thought that freedom would mean finding myself in a grocery store with a jar of tomato sauce in my hand, and no idea what to do next.

So I decided I would try to make lasagna, my first real stab at cooking. I figured that lasagna would be a friendly dish. Layers of noodles and sauce and cheese. What could go wrong? And I was so bold that I didn't even follow the recipe. I boiled the noodles for too long, didn't season the meat, spread the ricotta too haphazardly. The edges were burnt by the time I pulled the dish out of the oven, and the middle was cold. Everything fell apart when I tried to serve it. My lasagna looked like a collapsed building more than a dinner.

So I called my grandmother.

She picked up after three rings. I could hear the tv in the background. I explained my catastrophe. I expected her to laugh. Instead she asked, "Did you let the sauce simmer?"

"No."

"Did you cover it with foil?"

"No."

Then there was a silence. The kind that made me feel both stupid and special.

And she explained. How to brown the meat slowly. How to taste the sauce before you layer it. How to make sure there's enough liquid for the noodles to absorb. How to let the lasagna sit before you cut into it. No numbers. Instincts. "It's like listening. When you cook. You have to listen. You have to listen to what the food needs."

I scribbled her advice on the back of an unopened envelope. I knew that I would lose it one day. But the voice I remembered. How it sounded so sure, and patient, and came through the phone into my tiny kitchen. The unfamiliar kitchen.

My next lasagna wasn't perfect. The noodles were still a little too soft. I put too much cheese on it. But it stayed together. I sat at my small table. And I ate it by myself. But I was proud. Not so much of the food. More that I had learned that being independent wasn't the same thing as knowing everything. It was sometimes admitting that you didn't know. That you should call someone who does.

I make lasagna differently from my grandmother now. Years later. I measure some things. I guess at others. But when I taste my sauce I remember what she told me to do. Listen. Like being grown up. It's a matter of listening. Listening to the heat. Listening to the hunger. Listening to the mistakes. Listening to the voices who guide you.

Looking back at what I've reviewed (which is about 15 PRs a week), good code review is not about "how can I show off that I can spot issues" but about supporting the team in making the best decision fast. It's not about "show how much I know", but about improving the code while maintaining the author's momentum and feeling of ownership.

To do a good review I start by establishing context. Before diving into implementation details, I try to understand the problem the code is trying to solve, the behavior it's trying to achieve, and the constraints behind the change. A pretty technical solution might not be the right solution if it's solving the wrong problem or adding too much complexity. So I focus on architecture first, correctness, failure modes, security, performance, and maintainability. Only when those are clear do I dive into more superficial things like naming or formatting.

Give specific, actionable feedback with the right priority. I try to separate blocking issues from suggestions and personal preferences. Instead of "this looks fragile" I might say "there's a potential problem with this. When the input is empty, this might not work. Can we add a test or handle this case?". Also I try not to confuse my preferences with general principles. I'm not always commenting on every deviation from how I would implement the code. Too much nitpicking can distract from more important issues.

Tone matters too. The code review is a collaborative conversation. Not an exam. I try to ask questions if I'm not getting enough context. To explain my rationale for big issues. And highlight what's good. Positive feedback is not just about politeness. It helps highlight good patterns and give a sense to the author what they should keep doing.

Also, I try to be mindful of delays. Prompt review is a part of engineering quality, especially when you have a teammate who's waiting for the merge or for things to unblock. I try to comment in a way that helps advance the discussion. That definitively ends threads. That doesn't re-introduce things that were agreed on unless we have new information. The best outcome is not that each line of code looks how I would have it. But that the team is comfortable with the change. The author learned something. The code gets easier to evolve.

Goal: boost performance on our internal QA while tracking safety behavior

Base: 7B parameter model
Training: fine-tuning on our current task specific training set
Main metric: internal QA exact match
Secondary metric: safety eval score
Compare: Fine-tuned vs baseline (not fine-tuned)

Model Internal QA EM Safety Eval

Fine-tuned 7B model 66.8% -3% (lower)

5.6% more exact match (+5.6%) (61.2%->66.8%)
-3% lower on safety eval compared to baseline

Observations:

We see a clear improvement on our QA task in the fine-tuning experiment, but we are also seeing a (measurable) regression on our safety eval. This suggests some sort of trade-off between being task specific vs being safe.

What's going on?

Our training mix / objective is possibly too specific and focuses too much on the answer matching (answering questions correctly) at the cost of giving responses with safety concerns. This safety regression is likely a show-stopper until we understand it and fix it.

Next steps:

1. Look into safety eval failures and find patterns/categories for this regression
2. Investigate if fine-tuning data includes any examples that violate the safety guidelines.
3. Try safety preservation strategies (mix safety examples in fine-tuning? add safety weighted loss or preference? safety post training?)
4. Re-run the evals (on same checkpoint!) and make sure we have reliable results (statistically)
5. See if it's possible to have less boost on the QA but avoid the safety regression.

Remote work is heralded as the panacea. From my two years of mentoring 5 junior engineers, it's overblown for any juniors still learning how to code.

Jrs don't need tickets or documentation or meeting. They need to sit in on design conversations. They need to see how others debug issues. They need to ask questions before they have hours of confusion. That kind of interaction happens organically in an office. For remote work, they need to know the right times to cut in, set up a call, and to explain a problem that they might not even fully understand yet. It's a skill (and a tough one!) to have before you have a chance to learn it.

I've seen the feedback issues in remote work. Short comments on code review can feel like the final word instead of a learning opportunity. Also, it takes longer, so less momentum. The jrs I mentored typically improved faster if they had in person pairing, whiteboard sessions, etc. and had easy access to seniors.

I'm not trying to push for offices or anti-flexibility. Remote work can be great for self-driven devs. But for jrs, proximity is a booster that gives confidence, context, and instincts. Sending jrs off with a laptop and a calendar can be a drag on junior development which can result in less good technical leadership in the future.

Project Retrospective: Mobile App Launch

Project: Mobile App Launch
Original Launch Date: [Original Date]
Actual Launch Date: [Actual Date]
Schedule Variance: -2 weeks (late)
Retrospective Date: [Date]

1. Executive Summary

Mobile App launch was delayed 2 weeks. This was mainly due to:

1. App store review rejection requiring rework and re-submission cycle
 2. Late design change to onboarding that increased the scope of implementation/QA/localization work in the latter part of schedule

Overall, we were able to successfully deliver and launch the app. The launch quality was to the (new) expectations. No major post launch issues were reported. However, the project revealed gaps in our release readiness process, design change management and schedule contingencies.

2. What Happened

Development and initial round of QA went as planned per the schedule. Toward the latter part of the project

- There was a late change to the onboarding experience (to improve UX and product direction alignment)
 - This required more engineering work as well as new content and additional testing.
 - App submitted to app store but review revealed issues that led to rejection
 - We responded to feedback from review and prepared to re-submit with the necessary validation steps.
- All of this additional work used up the remaining schedule buffers and we ended up delaying the launch by ~2 weeks.

3. Impact

- We had to delay external availability by 2 weeks
- It required additional engineering, design, QA, release management effort
- Launch communications and corresponding marketing activities were rescheduled
- We had less time for post-launch monitoring before other work was scheduled
- It created additional stress in the team for the last bit of release

The core functionality of the app and the long-term roadmap weren't significantly impacted. But the confidence in the initial launch forecast was diminished by the delay.

4. Root Causes

4.1 App store review rejection

App store review rejected the app because it didn't meet certain review requirements fully. This was an unexpected outcome in our release plan. Our schedule didn't provide a contingency for rejection and re-submission cycle.

Some contributing factors were:

- Review requirements weren't validated early enough
- Release checklist was mostly focused on technical readiness instead of platform policy readiness
- We didn't consider the initial submission as feedback loop, more of a final validation
- There was limited buffer in the launch plan for external review dependencies.

4.2 Late change to onboarding design

We changed onboarding design late in the project in order to enhance user experience and better align with the product direction. While the change is valuable, it came in too late after the initial design/implementation work.

This change added work across

- UX / Visual design
- Engineering implementation
- Analytics & Event tracking
- Content and localization
- Accessibility validation
- Regression testing
- Product/Stakeholders review

Since the change was late in the schedule we couldn't really absorb all the work without impacting the launch date.

4.3 Gaps in planning/process

The two root causes mentioned above were magnified by planning gaps such as

- No explicit contingency for platform review delays in the schedule
- We didn't assess impact on launch date of late scope changes with a formal decision process
- Lack of clarity around release readiness criteria defined early in the project
- Some validation work happened sequentially instead of parallel
- Ownership of App store compliance review wasn't very explicit.

5. What went well

- We reacted quickly after we got the app store rejection.
- There was good collaboration between engineering/design/QA/product to address the rejection issues.
- The onboarding change didn't require a wider redesign of the app.
- QA was able to focus on regression coverage even under tight schedule
- We kept the stakeholders aware as launch risk increased
- We didn't try to ship critical issues known to us in order to make it for original date
- Final launch was stable and met the new quality bar.

6. What could have been better

- We should have reviewed app store policy/metadata requirements before final submission.
- We should have evaluated the change to onboarding redesign earlier or postpone it for a subsequent release.
- We should have had a better way to assess the impact on schedule for late changes.
- At least one contingency cycle for external review should have been part of the release plan.
- Design/implementation/content/analytics/QA dependencies weren't fully visible in initial plan.
- We should have had an early "scope freeze" date for launch critical work.

7. Corrective & Preventive Actions

| Corrective/Preventive Action | Owner | Priority | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Add App store policy/metadata review to release checklist | Release Manager | High | Before next submission |
| Pre-submission review using latest platform guidelines | Product/QA | High | For each release |
| Add explicit contingency for app store review & resubmission | Project Lead | High | Next release plan |
| Scope freeze date for launch | Product | High | At project kickoff |
| Design change impact assessment after scope freeze | Product/Design | High | Immediate |
| Onboarding analytics/accessibility requirement tracking during design review | Product/Design/Engineering | Medium | Next feature cycle |
| Final regression tests to run in parallel with release readiness checks (wherever possible) | QA/Engineering | Medium | Next release |
| Define launch readiness criteria and owners at project kickoff | Project Lead | High | Next project |
| Framework to defer non-critical late changes (decision doc) | Leadership/Product | Medium | Next planning cycle |

8. Key Learnings

1. Treat external approvals as schedule dependencies
- App store review isn't completely in our control so we need to have early validation and contingency time in plans

2. There is a cross-functional cost to late design changes
- A change that may look localized to onboarding might impact engineering/analytics/content/accessibility/QA/launch communications

3. Need a "scope freeze" for predictable launches
- Beyond scope freeze any changes should either be demonstrably critical to launch or should be pushed to a next release

4. Start release readiness before code complete.
- There should be a constant review of policy compliance, metadata, permissions, privacy disclosures and store assets.

5. It was the right call to protect the quality
- Even though we ended up delaying the launch, not shipping until review/product issues are resolved lead to more reliable launch.

9. Closing Assessment

Overall, we had a launch delay due to certain process/planning gaps (rather than specific team failures). Late change to onboarding increased scope of work to be done and the app store rejection caused an external review cycle that we couldn't absorb in the schedule. To make future launches more predictable without compromising product quality, we should focus on better validation of platform early in the process, better change management and explicit contingency planning.

That isn't a shift in some abstract public attitude. It is a direct response to having a place to ride that doesn't end in a hospital.

The math is simple once you see it. When you put a car sized barrier between the two groups, the car group stops trying to bully the other. You get a whole lot more people on two wheels without any of the usual safety theater. You are not asking for a change in behavior, you are just removing the reason that behavior was impossible in the first place. Other places that have tried to get the same result with signage and exhortation have mostly failed. The Paris numbers prove that the only thing that actually moves the needle is the physical separation of the two.

That kind of change also pays off in ways the traffic engineers usually miss. You get a city that is a bit easier to get around in when the roads are otherwise at their limit. The whole thing ends up working better for everyone, provided you are willing to give up a little of the old car first.

You could get a whole novel for sixpence. That was the trick Allen Lane pulled off in 1935 when he set up Penguin Books. The price was the same as a packet of cigarettes, and the books looked like it, with colored bands on the spine to sort out the genres. You got the same sort of thing you'd find in a more expensive shop. Some of it was popular fiction, some of it was pretty serious work. That mix did a lot to get rid of the notion that a cheap book had to be a bad one. You'd already seen the shape of the thing in the pamphlets and chapbooks of the past, and in the yellowbacks of the nineteenth century. But the modern version needed the whole package of mass printing, better paper, and a lot more people who could read. It got into the hands of people on the train, in the classroom, and just out for a walk.

The habit caught on fast, first in Britain and then in the United States and other places. That was mostly during and after the Second World War. The printers cranked out the novels, the biographies, the mysteries and romances, and the school books. A soldier, a student, or a working person could put together a library that way. Nobody else could have afforded the same collection. By the middle of the last century that had become the main way people got hold of books. You've still got it to hand now. The electronic versions have not quite managed to displace it. People still want the thing they can pick up and carry around.

You could get a whole library for the price of a few drinks before the 1930s. The trouble was that the books you got that way were mostly second hand or reprinted by some half starved little press. Penguin Books changed the whole game when they got going in that year. They sold out their first lot of eleven titles in a couple of months, and the reason was simple. You could pick up a copy for sixpence. That price tag put something like Shakespeare or a new novel in the pocket of a schoolboy. It wasn't so much that they were the first to print on cheaper paper as that they actually made that kind of thing something the general public wanted. The whole business of reading for pleasure got a lot more democratic from that point on.

That same sort of thing has happened a few times since. You see it now with the way digital files have got around the old printing costs. The sixpence price of 1935 was only the first time that the cost of getting hold of a book got separated from the cost of making it. You end up with a lot more people reading a lot more different things. None of the old established publishers had any real use for that sort of thing at first. They were quite happy to keep on selling their wares to a rather more limited set of customers.

You think you know what you're getting when you leave home at nineteen. You picture late mornings and an apartment you've got all to yourself. Nobody asking if you've eaten. Nobody to ask. What you don't picture is standing in a grocery aisle with a jar of tomato sauce and absolutely no idea what to do with it.

I picked lasagna for my first real try. It looked like it would forgive a lot. You just pile on noodles, sauce, and cheese. Who could screw that up? I was sure of myself enough to skip the recipe. The noodles got overcooked. The meat never got seasoned. The ricotta ended up in lopsided clumps. Out of the oven it came with burned edges and a cold middle. One fork and the whole thing fell apart. It was less a dinner than a collapsed building.

I called my grandmother. She got me on the third ring, some television going on behind her. I laid out the mess, half expecting a laugh. She just wanted to know if I had let the sauce simmer. I hadn't. Neither had I covered the thing with foil. That pause that followed made me feel pretty stupid, and oddly enough, pretty well taken care of.

She went on from there. Brown the meat slowly. Taste the sauce before you put it in. Leave enough liquid for the noodles to take in. Let the whole thing sit before you cut it. No measurements, just a set of instincts. Cooking is listening, she told me. The food tells you what it needs. I scribbled that down on the back of an unopened envelope. I knew the paper would end up in the trash. What got through was the sound of her, patient and sure, coming through the phone into that small kitchen of mine.

The second lasagna still came out with noodles a bit too soft and far too much cheese. It held together though. I sat down to it at my little table and felt a sort of pride that had nothing to do with the food. You don't have to know everything to get along. You just have to know when to call somebody who does.

I am still not making it the way she did. I measure some things and guess at the rest. But I stop to taste the sauce every time. That is what she got through. You have to pay attention to the heat, the hunger, the mistakes, and the people who help you out. That is as much part of it as the rest.

You get a lot of mileage out of asking what the code is supposed to do. I go through about 15 pull requests a week and the pattern is pretty clear. You aren't trying to prove you can spot every flaw. You are trying to get the team to a sound decision fast. That takes some of the ego out of it. You keep the author moving and let them keep ownership of the work.

You have to get the context right first. That means figuring out the problem, the intended behavior, and the constraints before you start poking at the implementation. A solution can be technically elegant and still be the wrong one. It solves the wrong problem or drags in a pile of extra complexity. I look at the architecture, the failure modes, security, and how well it will hold up. Naming and formatting only come in after all that is sorted out.

You also have to be straight about what you are saying. A note that says this may fail on empty input and asks for a test to cover that case is worth something. Saying it seems fragile is not. You have to keep the three kinds of comment you might have separate. The stuff that blocks a merge is different from a suggestion, and both are different from your own taste. You are not going to win by dressing up your style preferences as universal rules. The nitpicking ends up hiding the real trouble.

None of this works if the whole thing gets turned into an examination. It is a conversation. You ask questions when you are missing something, you explain the reasoning behind the big concerns, and you call out what works. That last part does more than keep things pleasant. It lets the author see which of their decisions are worth repeating.

The clock is part of the job too. A teammate is usually sitting on your response to get their own work unblocked. You get the discussion moving by settling the threads that have been raised. You do not go back and relitigate points that have already been decided. You have not done the job when every line of the code matches your own. You have done it when the team is confident in the change and the code is easier to work with going forward.

Nobody else in our family would have made that trip. You are getting a man who will do the same for you, only without the six hour drive. So let's raise a glass to him. He's earned it.

That passport story is probably the one to lead with. It gets the room to laugh right off the bat and then you can ease into the more sentimental stuff. The bunk bed bit works well as a quick aside to get the point across that he's always been the one looking out for you. You don't need to get into the finer details of either story. The numbers you have are plenty to make the point. Just make sure you have a drink in your hand for that last line.

You'll remember him for the one time he got away with it. Fourteen years of mostly well behaved sniffing, and then that one afternoon he got the whole rotisserie chicken off the counter. He didn't even try to hide it, just sat in the middle of the kitchen looking up at you with that stupid beagle face. That was the best of him, the way he could look you right in the eye and get off with it. You'll probably find yourself telling that story for a long time, and that is a pretty good thing to have to remember him by. He was a good dog, mostly, and you got to keep the best part of him.

You might get a little bit of that same feeling when you go to get a chicken from the store. It won't be the same, of course, but you'll be back in that kitchen with him. That single act of theft has outlasted the rest of his life in your memory, and I wouldn't trade that for a more spotless record. He got away with it once and that is plenty.

We got the app out the door, two weeks behind the date we'd been promising. You can't put that on the App Store, though. They bounced the first two submissions over a privacy disclosure we hadn't updated. That was mostly our fault since we'd built the feature without checking the current guidelines. The second hit came from the client, who decided the onboarding flow needed a full visual overhaul three days before we were ready to submit. We could have caught the first problem with an earlier pre check. The second one we just had to eat.

The privacy thing is easy to fix next time. It just means running a compliance pass before we ever get near a submission. The onboarding mess is harder to plan around. You either need to lock the design much further out or build in a schedule that can absorb that sort of thing. Neither of those options was on the table when we started. The result is that the whole team ended up working through a long weekend to get things in shape. We have the app now, but the cost of getting it there was pretty steep.

You get told remote work is a win for everybody. I've mentored five junior engineers for the last two years and it isn't. They don't need tickets, docs, or a set of scheduled meetings. What they need is to get in on design arguments, watch somebody else get through a nasty bug, and get answers before a little uncertainty snowballs. You get all of that for free in an office. Work from home and they have to figure out when to interrupt, get a call set up, and explain a problem they probably don't get yet. That is a pretty steep thing to ask of someone who hasn't had the chance to learn it.

I've watched that setup screw up feedback. A short note on a code review ends up reading like a final judgment, and the lag on getting answers kills any forward motion. The people I worked with moved ahead a lot quicker when they could pair up in person, work through things on a whiteboard, and actually get hold of the seniors. None of this means you should scrap flexibility. It works fine for people who can direct their own efforts. For a beginner, being around other people is what gets them there. It is how they pick up the confidence, context, and judgment they are going to need. You are going to end up with weaker technical leadership down the road if you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar.

You can't learn to code by watching someone else do it. I've been stuck in that trap for the last two years. Five of my juniors have come through my group, and every single one of them got stuck in the same way. You can send a screen share, you can post a long write up, you can set up a call. None of it gets at the thing you actually need. You need to see someone else get stuck, and you need to watch them work through it. That kind of learning just doesn't happen over a video link. You end up with a bunch of people who can follow a well documented path but who fall apart the moment things go off the rails.

The whole thing works fine for people who already know the ropes. They can get by with a few well timed check ins. A person who is still figuring out the basics needs to be in the same room. They need to interrupt, to ask the sort of question they might otherwise be too embarrassed to put into words. You can't get that sort of feedback from a chat window. I'd rather see a little more of my team's early work suffer for it than have them go on to make the same mistakes all over again.

# Mobile App Launch, What We Got Wrong

We got there two weeks after the date we'd been promising. The original launch date is in the record, and so is the actual one. You can work out the gap yourself. The App Store bounced the first submission, which forced a whole resubmission cycle. That would have been manageable on its own. The onboarding flow got a late redesign right when we thought we were done, and that change dragged engineering, QA, and localization out with it. We still got the thing out the door. It works the way we wanted it to and nobody has reported any major breakage since. The whole thing did put a pretty clear light on how badly we'd botched our release readiness.

You'd have thought the project was on track right up to the end. It was. Then the onboarding flow got its belated makeover. That meant new code, new content, and yet another pass through the test suite. We sent the result off to the App Store and got it back with a list of things to fix. The team went back in, sorted the complaints, and got a second version ready. All that work ate up the little bit of slack we'd kept in the schedule. Two weeks is what it cost.

That two week gap meant the outside world had to wait that much longer. It cost extra hours from the people doing the engineering and the checking. We had to go back and move the marketing and announcement work to match. There was less time left to watch how the thing behaved once it was out. Nobody got any relief from that last bit of pressure. You won't find any of this in the app's actual feature set or in what we have in mind for the future. It did take a fair bit of the faith we'd had in the first forecast.

The App Store rejection happened because the submission missed one or more of their rules. We had not built that possibility into the plan. We had not checked those rules early enough. The checklist we kept our eyes on was mostly about whether the code worked, not whether it fit the platform's policy. We went in thinking the first try would be the last. The onboarding change was a good one in the end. It just came in after the original work was already in place. It then forced additions to the visual design, the code, the event tracking, the localized content, the accessibility checks, and the regression tests. There was no way to take on all that near the end and keep the first date.

The two big problems got worse because we had not made room for them. We had no formal way to weigh a late change against the date we were trying to hit. The criteria for being ready to go had never been set down clearly. Some of the checking had to be done in a long line instead of at the same time. Nobody had been given a clear and final say over the compliance matters.

The team did get to work on the rejection issues right away. That first part went off without a hitch. The onboarding change got in without wrecking the rest of the app. The people doing the checking managed to keep their eye on the old parts of the thing. People outside the team kept getting the word as the risk grew. We had the sense to hold off on a launch that would have included known critical issues. What finally went out was a stable thing.

We should have gone over the store's rules before making that last submission. The onboarding work should have been looked at much earlier, or else left for a time when it could not do so much damage. We had no way to get a clear picture of how a late change would land. The first plan failed to show how all the separate parts depended on one another. A point at which the work to be done would be fixed should have been set down at the very start.

The next release checklist is going to have a place for the policy and metadata matters. That same pre submission check is to be made a regular part of the work. The plan for the next one is to carry an express allowance for the possibility of a bounce. We are to set the date for the work to be finished at the start of the project. Any change made after that point has to be shown to be absolutely necessary. The checking of the final product is to be done at the same time as the other readiness work. The decision of what to put off is to be made by some framework that is written down and available to all.

You have to plan for the outside approval work as if it were part of your own schedule. That kind of thing is not in your own hands. A change that seems to touch only the first few screens will end up reaching out to a great many other parts. You cannot get a date you can rely on without some point at which the work to be done is declared to be finished. The checking of the policy matters ought to have been going on long before the last of the code was in. Getting out a late but sound thing was the better of the two choices we had.

The whole thing came about from a set of gaps in the way we went about it. It was not the fault of any one person. The late change made the remaining work larger, and the outside rejection then added a cycle the plan had no way to take in. Getting the outside checks done earlier and holding the changes to a tighter rein ought to get us to a more reliable way of doing this.
